First, we verify that $\mathscr{d}_\pi$ is well-defined on the quotient space $\mathscr{T}^\pi(X)$. Let $\bm{x}, \bm{x}^\prime \in \bm{x}^\pi$ and $\bm{y}, \bm{y}^\prime \in \bm{y}^\pi$ be representatives of two equivalence classes. If $\ell(\bm{x}) \neq \ell(\bm{y})$, then $\ell(\bm{x}^\prime) = \ell(\bm{x}) \neq \ell(\bm{y}) = \ell(\bm{y}^\prime)$, so both evaluations yield $1$. If $\ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\bm{y}) = 0$, both evaluations yield $0$. Suppose therefore that $\ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\bm{y}) = n > 0$. By Definition~\ref{defn:permutative-equality}, there exist permutations $\alpha, \beta \in \mathscr{P}_n$ such that $\bm{x}^\prime = \bm{x} \circ \alpha$ and $\bm{y}^\prime = \bm{y} \circ \beta$. For any candidate matching $\sigma \in \mathscr{P}_n$, reindexing $j = \alpha(i)$ yields
    \begin{align*}
        \max_{i \in \{1, \dots, n\}} \bar{d}\big(\bm{x}^\prime(i), \bm{y}^\prime(\sigma(i))\big)
        &= \max_{i \in \{1, \dots, n\}} \bar{d}\big(\bm{x}(\alpha(i)), \bm{y}(\beta(\sigma(i)))\big)\\
        &= \max_{j \in \{1, \dots, n\}} \bar{d}\big(\bm{x}(j), \bm{y}((\beta \circ \sigma \circ \alpha^{-1})(j))\big).
    \end{align*}
    Since $\sigma \mapsto \beta \circ \sigma \circ \alpha^{-1}$ is a bijection of $\mathscr{P}_n$ onto itself, taking the minimum over $\sigma \in \mathscr{P}_n$ yields the same value for $(\bm{x}^\prime, \bm{y}^\prime)$ as for $(\bm{x}, \bm{y})$. Thus $\mathscr{d}_\pi$ does not depend on the chosen representatives.
steps.title: Proof step 1

steps.text:
Next, we must show that $\mathscr{d}_\pi : \mathscr{T}^\pi(X) \times \mathscr{T}^\pi(X) \to [0, 1]$ satisfies the three criteria of a metric for all $\bm{x}^\pi, \bm{y}^\pi, \bm{z}^\pi \in \mathscr{T}^\pi(X)$:
    \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
        \item $\mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{x}^\pi, \bm{y}^\pi) = 0$ if and only if $\bm{x}^\pi = \bm{y}^\pi$.
        \item $\mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{x}^\pi, \bm{y}^\pi) = \mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{y}^\pi, \bm{x}^\pi)$.
        \item $\mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{x}^\pi, \bm{z}^\pi) \leq \mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{x}^\pi, \bm{y}^\pi) + \mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{y}^\pi, \bm{z}^\pi)$.
    \end{enumerate}

Proof step 3

steps.text:
For (b), the claim is immediate when $\ell(\bm{x}) \neq \ell(\bm{y})$ or $\ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\bm{y}) = 0$. For $\ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\bm{y}) = n > 0$, symmetry of $\bar{d}$ and the bijection $\sigma \mapsto \sigma^{-1}$ on $\mathscr{P}_n$ give
    \begin{align*}
        \mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{x}^\pi, \bm{y}^\pi)
        &= \min_{\sigma \in \mathscr{P}_n} \max_{i \in \{1, \dots, n\}} \bar{d}\big(\bm{x}(i), \bm{y}(\sigma(i))\big)\\
        &= \min_{\sigma \in \mathscr{P}_n} \max_{j \in \{1, \dots, n\}} \bar{d}\big(\bm{y}(j), \bm{x}(\sigma^{-1}(j))\big)
        = \mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{y}^\pi, \bm{x}^\pi).
    \end{align*}
steps.title: Proof step 4

steps.text:
For (c), if $\ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\bm{y}) = \ell(\bm{z}) = n > 0$, let $\sigma, \sigma^\prime \in \mathscr{P}_n$ attain the minima defining $\mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{x}^\pi, \bm{y}^\pi)$ and $\mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{y}^\pi, \bm{z}^\pi)$, respectively. Since $\sigma^\prime \circ \sigma \in \mathscr{P}_n$, the triangle inequality for $\bar{d}$ yields
    \begin{align*}
        \mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{x}^\pi,\bm{z}^\pi)
        &\leq \max_{i \in \{1, \dots, n\}} \bar{d}\big(\bm{x}(i),\bm{z}(\sigma^\prime(\sigma(i)))\big)\\
        &\leq \max_{i \in \{1, \dots, n\}} \bar{d}\big(\bm{x}(i),\bm{y}(\sigma(i))\big) + \max_{i \in \{1, \dots, n\}} \bar{d}\big(\bm{y}(\sigma(i)),\bm{z}(\sigma^\prime(\sigma(i)))\big)\\
        &= \mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{x}^\pi,\bm{y}^\pi) + \mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{y}^\pi,\bm{z}^\pi).
    \end{align*}
    If $\ell(\bm{x}) \neq \ell(\bm{z})$, then $\mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{x}^\pi, \bm{z}^\pi) = 1$, while either $\ell(\bm{x}) \neq \ell(\bm{y})$ or $\ell(\bm{y}) \neq \ell(\bm{z})$, so at least one of $\mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{x}^\pi, \bm{y}^\pi)$ or $\mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{y}^\pi, \bm{z}^\pi)$ equals $1$. If $\ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\bm{z})$ but $\ell(\bm{y}) \neq \ell(\bm{x})$, then $\mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{x}^\pi, \bm{z}^\pi) \leq 1 < 2 = \mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{x}^\pi, \bm{y}^\pi) + \mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{y}^\pi, \bm{z}^\pi)$. Finally, if $\ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\bm{y}) = \ell(\bm{z}) = 0$, all three distances are $0$. Therefore, $(\mathscr{T}^\pi(X), \mathscr{d}_\pi)$ is a metric space.

    Let $(\mathcal{H},\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ be a real Hilbert space, write $\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})=\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H})$, and let $T\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})$.
    \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
        \item The adjoint of $T$ is the operator $T^\ast\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})$ such that $\langle Tu,v\rangle=\langle u,T^\ast v\rangle$ for all $u,v\in\mathcal{H}$, and $T$ is called self-adjoint if $T^\ast=T$.
        \item The operator $T$ has finite rank if its image $T(\mathcal{H})$ is finite-dimensional.
        \item The operator $T$ is called compact if the closure of $\{Tv\mid v\in\mathcal{H},\ \lVert v\rVert\leq1\}$ is compact. We write $\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{H})$ for the set of compact operators in $\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})$.
    \end{enumerate}

results.statement:
\label{rem:lp-point-evaluation}
    We obtain an operation on $L^p$ from representatives only when the operation is invariant under almost-everywhere equality. For Lebesgue measure, or any diffuse measure, on an interval, point evaluation fails this criterion, since two representatives of the same class may differ at a prescribed singleton. We therefore cannot assign a generic $L^p$ class a well-defined point value, canonical graph, or graph inverse. To use such operations, we fix (a) a selected regular representative; (b) a continuous subclass on which the natural map into $L^p$ is injective; (c) a c\`adl\`ag (respectively c\`agl\`ad) representative together with its terminal (respectively initial) value, which is lost by passage to $L^p$; or (d) a finite-dimensional parametrisation with a well-defined inverse.

    Let $(S,\mathcal{S},\mu)$ and $(T,\mathcal{T},\nu)$ be $\sigma$-finite measure spaces, and let $f:S\times T \to [-\infty,\infty]$ be $\mathcal{S}\otimes\mathcal{T}$-measurable, with $[-\infty,\infty]$ carrying its Borel $\sigma$-algebra.
    \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
        \item If $f \geq 0$, then the partial integrals are measurable and
        \begin{align*}
            \int_{S\times T} f \,\mathrm{d}(\mu \otimes \nu)
            &=
            \int_S \left(\int_T f(s,t)\,\mathrm{d}\nu(t)\right)\mathrm{d}\mu(s)
            \\
            &=
            \int_T \left(\int_S f(s,t)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(s)\right)\mathrm{d}\nu(t).
        \end{align*}
        \item If $\int_{S\times T} |f|\,\mathrm{d}(\mu \otimes \nu)<\infty$, then $f(s,\cdot)$ and $f(\cdot,t)$ are integrable for $\mu$- and $\nu$-almost every section respectively, the partial integrals, set to $0$ on the exceptional null sets, are measurable and integrable, and the identities in (i) hold for $f$.
    \end{enumerate}

We prove the three claims in order. For (i), since $[0]\in\mathcal{C}$, the set is non-empty; it is convex because convex combinations of non-decreasing functions with values in $[0,1]$ are again non-decreasing with values in $[0,1]$. For closedness, suppose $[f_n]\in\mathcal{C}$ and $[f_n]\to[f]$ in $L^2([a,b])$. Choose bounded non-decreasing representatives of $[f_n]$ and a subsequence converging almost everywhere to a representative of $[f]$. On the full-measure convergence set, the limit is non-decreasing; its monotone extension to $[a,b]$, obtained from one-sided suprema and endpoint limits, agrees with that representative almost everywhere and remains in $[0,1]$. Hence $[f]\in\mathcal{C}$. Because $\mathcal{C}$ is non-empty, closed, and convex in the Hilbert space $L^2([a,b])$, its metric projection $P_{\mathcal{C}}:L^2([a,b])\to\mathcal{C}$ exists, is unique at the equivalence-class level, and is $1$-Lipschitz.

    For (ii), with $G_s$ as above and $u\in L^2([a,b])$, let $h_u(y)=\int_a^b u(x)\mathbbm{1}\{y\leq x\}\,\mathrm{d}x$. Since $\langle\mathbb{E}[\chi_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s],u\rangle=\mathbb{E}[\langle\chi_t,u\rangle\mid\mathcal{F}_s]$ almost surely, Fubini's theorem for the kernel $\kappa_s$ gives $\langle\mathbb{E}[\chi_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s],u\rangle=\mathbb{E}[h_u(X_t)\mid\mathcal{F}_s]=\int_a^b u(x)G_s(\cdot,x)\,\mathrm{d}x$ almost surely. Applying this to a countable dense subset of $L^2([a,b])$ and discarding countably many null sets gives $\mathbb{E}[\chi_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]=[G_s(\cdot,\cdot)|_{[a,b]}]$ almost surely. Since each $G_s(\omega,\cdot)$ is a distribution function, $\mathbb{E}[\chi_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]\in\mathcal{C}$ almost surely.

    For (iii), for any $[f]\in\mathcal{C}$, the selected extension $\mathsf{S}([f])$ is non-decreasing and right-continuous, has limits $0$ and $1$ at $-\infty$ and $+\infty$, and may assign masses at $a$ and $b$; it therefore lies in $\mathfrak{D}_{[a,b]}$. By construction, $\mathsf{S}$ is the inverse of the restriction map $F\mapsto[F|_{[a,b]}]$ from $\mathfrak{D}_{[a,b]}$ to $\mathcal{C}$, so the $L^2([a,b])$ encoding of distribution functions supported on $[a,b]$ is injective. Since any two distribution functions $F,G\in\mathfrak{D}_{[a,b]}$ agree outside $[a,b)$, their Cram\'er distance $(\int_{\mathbb{R}}(F-G)^2\,\mathrm{d}x)^{1/2}$ equals $\lVert[F|_{[a,b]}]-[G|_{[a,b]}]\rVert_{L^2([a,b])}$, which proves that $\mathsf{S}$ is an isometry.
